newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's conservatives carry on despite ETA threats.
newsitem.headline: Spain's conservatives carry on despite ETA threats.

text.p: Spain's ruling conservatives, long targeted by ETA as the Basque separatist rebel group's worst enemies, vowed on Tuesday to carry on despite a new death threat days after a young party member was killed.
"We already know that the Popular Party is a target for ETA," Angel Acebes, general coordinator of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's party, told a news conference.
"For all the threats they make, for all the harm they try to cause, they are not going to make us renounce our objectives."

Acebes, speaking after a special meeting of the party's executive with Aznar, said the Popular Party would join forces with all other political parties to implement specific measures to bolster the fight against ETA after the killing.

Separatist guerrillas kidnapped Miguel Angel Blanco, a Popular Party (PP) town councillor in the Basque region, on Thursday and said they would kill him if the government did not move all 500 ETA prisoners to the Basque region by Saturday.
The government called the threat blackmail and said it would not give in. ETA shot Blanco shortly after the deadline passed despite massive nationwide protest. He died on Sunday.
One day after Blanco was found dumped by a roadside with two gunshot wounds in his head, a bulls-eye target with the name of another Basque town councillor was spray-painted on his house.

Graffiti saying "You will be next" appeared beneath the bulls-eye target at the home of Jose Luis Caso, 63, in Renteria near San Sebastian on Monday. Another target alongside held the name of the party.
The PP official tried to shrug it off.
"I don't want to worry about it too much because I know that defending certain ideas in the Basque country carries a risk," he told newspaper El Pais.
Aznar himself narrowly survived an ETA car bomb attack in 1995 and remains a key target, according to newspaper reports.
A former ETA hostage reportedly testified on Monday that his captors had told him they were keen to assassinate the 44-year-old PP leader and that they would try again.
In statements made through radical Basque newspaper Egin, its usual mouthpiece, ETA has made it clear they consider the Popular Party their worst enemy.
"We have carried out this attack on Aznar as the highest representative of the re-installation in Spain of Francoism," ETA said when it claimed responsibility in 1995.

That same year, when it looked likely that Aznar's party would win the next election and become the first right-wing government since Franco, ETA shot and killed the party's leader in the Basque region, Gregorio Ordonez.
